subject: paediatrics
title: Kawasaki Disease, Coronary Aneurysms and Pediatric SVT

steps.tx: Acute necrotizing systemic medium-vessel vasculitis predominantly targets infants and toddlers. The foremost cause of acquired pediatric heart disease in developed nations is **Kawasaki disease vasculitis**, typically affecting children between six months and five years of age. Pan-arteritis of medium-sized muscular arteries triggers coronary arterial wall elastin destruction, predisposing up to twenty-five percent of untreated patients to progressive coronary aneurysm formation.
steps.say: Kawasaki disease is an acute medium-vessel vasculitis affecting children under five years. It causes pan-arteritis that damages coronary artery walls, predisposing to coronary aneurysms.

vis.alt: Clinical diagnostic criteria and manifestations of acute Kawasaki disease.
vis.caption: Diagnostic hallmarks of Kawasaki disease showing conjunctival injection, mucosal changes, rash, and coronary aneurysms. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Diagnostic classification requires fulfilling standardized clinical criteria centered upon protracted fever. Classic diagnosis demands **fever of five days duration** refractory to standard antipyretics, alongside at least four of five principal clinical criteria: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral mucosal changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips), polymorphous exanthem, peripheral extremity induration followed by periungual peeling, and acute non-purulent cervical lymphadenopathy exceeding 1.5 cm.
steps.say: Diagnose Kawasaki disease when fever persists for five days with four of five signs: non-exudative red eyes, strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, swollen hands, and a large cervical node.

steps.tx: In this short axis echo view a coronary artery has blown out into a sac far wider than any vessel its age should be. That **coronary aneurysm** is the feared residue of Kawasaki disease, where arteritis weakens the wall during the febrile weeks of early childhood. Echocardiographers measure and z score these dilatations because their size dictates antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy and lifelong cardiology follow up. Giant aneurysms rarely shrink back, so a childhood fever illness can schedule appointments for an adult decades later.
steps.say: A saccular coronary aneurysm on echo is the serious cardiac residue that Kawasaki disease surveillance hunts for.

vis.alt: Transthoracic echocardiogram parasternal short axis view showing saccular coronary artery aneurysm in left anterior descending artery
vis.caption: Transthoracic echocardiogram parasternal short axis view showing saccular coronary artery aneurysm in left anterior descending artery. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Echocardiographic monitoring evaluates progressive luminal dilatation of the coronary circulation. Untreated vasculitis provokes **coronary artery aneurysm formation**, peaking between two and four weeks after fever onset. Luminal dimensions are classified using body surface area Z-scores: Z-scores between 2.0 and 2.5 indicate dilation, 2.5 to 5.0 indicate small aneurysms, 5.0 to 10.0 represent medium aneurysms, and Z-scores of ten or greater (or absolute diameter >=8 mm) define giant aneurysms.
steps.say: Coronary artery aneurysms peak between two and four weeks after fever onset. Giant aneurysms with diameters of eight millimetres or greater carry high risks of thrombosis and myocardial infarction.

left.title: Small to Medium Aneurysms
points: Z-score between 2.5 and 10.0 (diameter <8 mm)
Frequently regress over 1 to 2 years
Low risk of acute thrombotic occlusion
Maintain daily low-dose antiplatelet aspirin

right.title: Giant Coronary Aneurysms
points: Z-score >=10.0 or internal diameter >=8 mm
High risk of rupture, thrombosis, and infarction
Rarely regress; develop calcification and stenosis
Requires dual antiplatelet therapy plus anticoagulation

steps.tx: Prompt biological therapy suppresses coronary inflammation and prevents permanent arterial aneurysms. Administering high-dose **intravenous immunoglobulin IVIG therapy** at a single dose of two grams per kilogram infused over ten to twelve hours within the first ten days of fever onset reduces coronary aneurysm incidence from twenty-five percent to under five percent. High-dose oral aspirin (80 to 100 mg/kg/day) is administered concurrently until the child is afebrile.
steps.say: A single infusion of intravenous immunoglobulin at two grams per kilogram given within ten days reduces coronary aneurysm risk below five percent. Combine with high-dose aspirin initially.

steps.tx: Enteroviral infection of cardiac myocytes provokes fulminant acute congestive heart failure in infants. Viral myocarditis, most commonly triggered by Coxsackievirus B or adenovirus, presents with sudden onset **myocarditis congestive heart failure**, characterized by poor feeding, lethargy, cool extremities, gallop rhythm (S3/S4), and unexplained cardiomegaly. Cardiac troponin I and brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) are elevated, and echocardiography reveals diffuse left ventricular hypokinesia.
steps.say: Viral myocarditis from Coxsackievirus causes acute infant heart failure, gallop rhythm, and low ejection fraction. Serum cardiac troponins and brain natriuretic peptide are markedly elevated.

left.title: Viral Myocarditis Profile
points: Sudden acute heart failure after viral illness
Elevated cardiac troponin I and NT-proBNP
Echocardiogram: globally depressed LV ejection (<30%)
Requires inotropes (milrinone) and ACE inhibitors

right.title: Dilated Cardiomyopathy Contrast
points: Insidious progressive left ventricular dilation
Familial genetic mutations (titin, lamin)
Normal inflammatory markers; absent troponin spike
Candidate for long-term ventricular assist device

steps.tx: Re-entrant electrical circuits via accessory conduction pathways provoke paroxysmal rapid narrow-complex tachycardias. The most prevalent symptomatic pathological arrhythmia in pediatrics is **supraventricular tachycardia arrhythmia** (SVT), presenting in infants with sudden heart rates between 220 and 300 beats per minute without beat-to-beat variability. Prolonged uncorrected SVT exceeding twenty-four to forty-eight hours causes secondary congestive heart failure, hepatomegaly, and cardiogenic shock.
steps.say: Supraventricular tachycardia causes sudden narrow-complex heart rates of 220 to 300 beats per minute in infants. Prolonged episodes precipitate secondary congestive heart failure.

rows: Narrow QRS (<0.09s), rate 220-300 bpm, P waves hidden
Vagal: ice to face; IV Adenosine push
Narrow QRS, severe hypotension, delayed capillary refill
Normal P waves preceding every QRS, rate <220
Treat underlying cause; never use adenosine
Short PR interval, delta wave, wide QRS baseline

steps.tx: Physical vagal maneuvers stimulate parasympathetic slowing of atrioventricular nodal conduction. In haemodynamically stable infants with SVT, initial bedside management applies **vagal stimulation ice application**, placing an ice-water filled plastic bag firmly over the infant's forehead and nose for ten to fifteen seconds to trigger the mammalian dive reflex. Clinicians must never perform ocular pressure in children due to high risks of retinal detachment.
steps.say: In stable infants with SVT, apply an ice bag over the nose and forehead for fifteen seconds to trigger the diving reflex. Never apply ocular pressure in children.

left.title: Effective Vagal Techniques
points: Crushed ice in plastic bag over face for 10-15 sec
Triggers mammalian dive reflex slowing AV node
Valsalva maneuver in older children (blowing into syringe)
Safe, rapid, non-pharmacological conversion in 50%

right.title: Dangerous Ineffective Techniques
points: Eyeball/ocular pressure (risks retinal detachment)
Bilateral carotid sinus massage in young infants
Immersing infant's entire head into cold water
Never delay medical pharmacotherapy if vagal fails

steps.tx: Purinergic receptor activation transiently blocks atrioventricular nodal electrical conduction. If vagal maneuvers fail, the pharmacological drug of choice is **rapid intravenous adenosine push**, administered at 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 6 mg) followed immediately by a rapid five-millilitre saline flush through an antecubital vein. Adenosine hyperpolarizes AV nodal tissue, breaking the re-entrant circuit within ten seconds; if the patient is haemodynamically unstable, immediate synchronized cardioversion (0.5 to 1 J/kg) is performed.
steps.say: Intravenous adenosine at 0.1 mg/kg rapid push followed by a saline flush terminates SVT by blocking the AV node. Unstable infants require immediate synchronized electrical cardioversion.

rows: Purinergic A1 receptor AV nodal block
Use three-way stopcock, proximal IV, rapid flush
Double dose if 1st dose fails at 2 min
Mandatory if hypotensive shock is present
